questions.q: If a protocol's docs and its verified on-chain contract disagree about how something works, which one actually governs what happens?
options: The docs always govern, since they're the official explanation
Whichever one was published more recently
Neither — a third party must arbitrate the disagreement
The verified on-chain contract, since it's the only one actually enforced by code
questions.explain: Docs describe an idealized version of the protocol; the deployed contract's code is what's actually enforced when you interact with it.

questions.q: What distinguishes a "Read" function from a "Write" function on a verified contract?
options: Read functions report state with no gas cost and no signature; Write functions change state and require a signed, gas-paying transaction
Read functions cost gas and Write functions are free
Read functions can only be called by the contract's admin
There is no real difference between the two
questions.explain: getReserves() or balanceOf() just report current state for free; swap() or mint() actually change state and require you to sign and pay gas.

questions.q: Why does being able to call getReserves() or balanceOf() yourself matter?
options: It allows you to change the contract's admin key
It lets you independently verify a pool's reserves or your balance without trusting any front-end's claim
It is required before any Write function can be called
It guarantees the contract has been professionally audited
questions.explain: Read functions let you check the contract's actual state directly, rather than taking a website's word for it.

questions.q: What is a timelock, in the context of a contract's admin controls?
options: A feature that prevents any transaction from ever reverting
A mechanism that locks user funds permanently
A mandatory delay between an admin proposing a change and it taking effect, giving users time to exit if they disagree
A requirement that only the original deployer can ever call any function
questions.explain: A timelock gives the community visibility and a window to react — e.g. withdraw funds — before an admin-proposed change actually takes effect.

questions.q: Why is a single, non-multisig admin key considered a red flag when evaluating a protocol?
options: Because single admin keys are illegal in most jurisdictions
Because multisig wallets cannot hold any funds
Because a single key always means the contract has not been audited
Because a single key can change contract behavior unilaterally, with no second party required to approve the change
questions.explain: A multisig requires multiple independent signers to agree before a change takes effect; a single key means one compromised or malicious actor can act alone.
